title: Lefkowitz v. Great Minneapolis Surplus Store
shortTitle: Lefkowitz v. Great Minneapolis Surplus Store
summary: A newspaper advertisement that names the item, the price, the time and the first person entitled to buy is a definite offer accepted by appearing first and tendering the price; the advertiser cannot then impose a house rule, such as “women only,” that the advertisement never stated.

sections.Parties: Morris Lefkowitz, the customer and plaintiff, was the respondent on appeal and represented himself. Great Minneapolis Surplus Store, Inc., the merchant and defendant, appealed an order refusing to amend the trial court’s findings or grant a new trial. Justice Murphy wrote for the Supreme Court of Minnesota on December 20, 1957.
sections.Material Facts: The store ran two advertisements a week apart. On April 6, 1956 it advertised three new fur coats “worth to $100” for one dollar each, available at 9 a.m. the following Saturday, first come first served. On April 13 it advertised two pastel mink three-skin scarfs described as selling for $89.50 and one black lapin stole “worth $139.50” for one dollar each, again at 9 a.m. Saturday, first come first served. On each Saturday Lefkowitz arrived first at the counter, demanded the advertised item and said he was ready to pay one dollar. The store refused both times: on the first visit it invoked an internal house rule limiting the offer to women, and on the second it relied on his knowledge of that rule from the previous week. Neither advertisement mentioned the restriction.
sections.Procedural History: Lefkowitz sued for breach of contract in the Municipal Court of Minneapolis. The court denied recovery for the coats because the only evidence of their value was the indefinite “worth to $100,” but accepted the stole’s stated value of $139.50 and awarded that sum less the one-dollar price, $138.50. The store moved for amended findings or a new trial; the municipal court denied the motion, and the store appealed that denial. The Supreme Court of Minnesota affirmed, leaving the $138.50 award in place. There was no dissent.
sections.Issue: Did the advertisement commit the store to sell on the stated terms once a customer performed the requested acts, or merely invite customers to make offers the store could refuse? Did Lefkowitz’s arrival and offer to pay accept it, and could the store enforce its unstated women-only rule afterward?
sections.Holding: Ordinary advertisements often invite offers, but an advertisement that is clear, definite and explicit and leaves nothing open for negotiation is an offer, and performance of its terms forms a contract. The stole advertisement identified the article, an exact price, the time and the eligible purchaser by order of arrival, so it was an offer; Lefkowitz accepted by arriving first and offering the price. Having accepted, he could not be met with new or arbitrary conditions absent from the published offer, and his prior knowledge of the house rule did not write it into the second advertisement. The award of $138.50 was affirmed.
sections.Reasoning: The legal character of an advertisement depends on its language and circumstances. Here the terms supplied both the store’s obligation and the person entitled to enforce it: one stole, one dollar, 9 a.m. Saturday, first come first served. Those terms also answered the usual objection to treating advertisements as offers, that a merchant might be bound beyond its stock, because the quantity and the taker were fixed. Lefkowitz accepted by doing exactly what the offer requested. An advertiser may modify or withdraw an offer before acceptance, but it cannot impose new or arbitrary conditions afterward, and the women-only rule was such a condition because the advertisement never stated it. The court resolved the case on the terms and timing of formation and did not treat it as a sex-discrimination claim. It also separated liability from proof of loss: the coats’ stated maximum of $100 did not establish what any coat was worth, so that claim failed for uncertain valuation, while the stole’s definite stated value supported an award of the value less the price.

priorVersions.summary: A definite, limited, first-come advertisement could be accepted on its stated terms; an undisclosed house rule could not be added afterward.

Court: Supreme Court of Minnesota (1957).

The notes compare Leonard’s reservations and missing limits, Geismar’s statutory consumer remedy despite no contract, auctions, and the Mint coin problem. A general statement that advertisements are never offers would misstate this unit.

sections.Parties: Lefkowitz, the first customer to respond, sued the surplus store that advertised fur items at a $1 price.
sections.Material Facts: An initial advertisement offered three coats “worth to $100”; a later one offered a black lapin stole worth $139.50 for $1, first come, first served. Lefkowitz arrived first and offered the price. The store refused to sell under a purported women-only house rule absent from the advertisements.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court awarded $138.50 for the stole and denied recovery for the coats because their value was speculative. The Minnesota Supreme Court affirmed the order denying the store’s request for amended findings or a new trial.
sections.Issue: Did the advertisement leave the seller free to accept or reject an offer from a shopper, or was it itself sufficiently definite to invite completion of a contract by performance?
sections.Holding: The stole advertisement was an offer, and Lefkowitz accepted it. The store could not impose a new condition after acceptance.
sections.Reasoning: The stated item, price, and first-come limitation left nothing open for negotiation. That limitation addressed the concern that treating an advertisement as an offer might create obligations beyond available supply. The first advertisement’s damages problem is distinct from the general question whether advertisements can be offers. The notes further ask how notice from the first refusal should affect analysis of the later transaction.

topics.offer: The advertisement was sufficiently definite to confer a power of acceptance.
topics.assent: The specified conduct communicated acceptance of the offer as published.
topics.performance-acceptance: Arriving first and offering the price completed the requested response.
topics.expectation: The award used the item’s established value less its contract price.
topics.notice: An unstated restriction was not added after acceptance.
